stem: Six stiff card pieces made a bridge. Use the same six pieces to make a different object. Draw it and label all six pieces. Then write how one piece's shape or stiffness helps its new job.
answer: A different object built from the same six pieces, all six drawn and labeled. One piece's shape or stiffness is linked to the job it does, with because or so. Access observation, no score: record a missing-piece gap (M) and a property-use gap (P) separately.
steps: a different object from the bridge, drawn with all six pieces labeled, none missing and none added | the writing links a piece's shape or stiffness to the job it does, with because or so, not only that stiff is good
samples: I made a ramp. Pieces 1 to 6 are labeled. Piece 1 is long and stiff, so it does not bend under a toy car. | I made a house from five pieces. Stiff is good for a house.

stem: A bottle that looks empty is pushed mouth down into water. A little water goes in. Tilted, it bubbles and fills. (a) Draw what filled it before it was tilted. (b) Plan 1: weigh a ball, pump air into it, weigh it again. Plan 2: weigh a flat ball and a different pumped ball. Finish: Plan ___ is fair because ___.
answer: (a) Air filled the bottle before it was tilted; dots are allowed but not required today. (b) Plan 1, because it is the same ball before and after the pumping, so only the air added differs.
steps: (a) the drawing shows something, such as air, bubbles or dots, filling the bottle before the tilt, not an empty bottle | (b) chooses Plan 1, the same ball weighed before and after air is pumped in | (b) the reason says only the air differs, or that the ball is the same
samples: I drew bubbles of air inside the bottle. Plan 1, because it is the same ball so only the air is different. | I drew an empty bottle. Plan 2.

stem: Six card pieces made a gate and are rebuilt as a shelf. Draw the shelf with all six pieces. Finish: Stiff card helps because ___.
answer: All six pieces appear in the shelf, none left out and none added. Stiff card keeps the shelf boards from bending under the books.
steps: six pieces drawn, none left out and none added | the sentence links the stiff card to the job: the boards do not bend, so the shelf holds the books
samples: I drew six boards: two sides, three shelves and a back. Stiff card helps because it does not bend, so the boards hold the books up. | I drew five pieces. Stiff card helps because stiff is good.

stem: A damp cloth weighs 64 g. Dried on a rack, it weighs 52 g. Water: ___ g. Cloth itself: ___ g.
answer: Water 12 g. The cloth itself 52 g. Dry it first, so water is not counted as the cloth.
steps: water lost = 64 - 52 = 12 g | dried cloth = 52 g
samples: Water 12 g; cloth itself 52 g. | Water 64 g; cloth itself 64 g.

stem: A book flattens a pouch of air. Puffed, it has 9 dots. Draw it flat. Finish: Flat, it has ___ dots.
answer: The flat pouch shows all 9 dots, packed closer together in less space. The air did not go away.
steps: 9 dots in the flat pouch, none erased | the dots are closer together than in the puffed pouch | the blank says 9
samples: Flat pouch: 9 dots packed close together in a small space. Flat, it has 9 dots. | Flat pouch: 5 dots. Flat, it has 5 dots. Some air went away.

stem: Finish: A stick moved to shade is unfair because ___.
answer: A stick moved to shade makes a different shadow for a reason other than the sun, so next month's reading cannot be compared. The stick, the mark and the clock time stay the same.
steps: says the moved stick changes the shadow, so a difference would not come from the sun | or names what must stay fixed: the same stick, the same mark, the same clock time
samples: ...because the shade makes a different shadow, so we cannot tell if it is the sun. | ...because it is fine to move it. It is the same stick.

stem: A sealed bottle gives when squeezed. Its air is 8 dots in a wide box. Draw the squeezed air. Finish: Squeezed, it has ___ dots.
answer: The same 8 dots, closer together in less space. The air did not go away.
steps: 8 dots in the squeezed drawing, the same number as before | the dots are closer together or in a smaller space | the blank says 8
samples: Squeezed: 8 dots packed closer in a smaller box. Squeezed, it has 8 dots. | Squeezed: no dots. Squeezed, it has 0 dots. There is no air in a bottle that gives.

stem: Jo zeroes an empty jar. A stone brings the reading to 58 g. A cutting brings it to 60 g. Water brings it to 86 g. Added: stone ___ g, cutting ___ g, water ___ g.
answer: Stone 58 g, cutting 2 g, water 26 g. Each line is what was added, not the running reading.
steps: stone 58 g | cutting 60 - 58 = 2 g | water 86 - 60 = 26 g
samples: Stone 58 g; cutting 2 g; water 26 g. | Stone 58 g; cutting 60 g; water 86 g.

stem: Case A: A packing cushion is full of air and sealed. A book is set on it. The cushion flattens but stays sealed. Case B: A sealed pouch holds water. Inside is a small packet of a solid that dissolves. The packet opens. The solid spreads out, and the water turns clear. (a) Draw the cushion before and after the book. (b) Draw the pouch before and after the packet opens. Use dots for parts too small to see. (c) Explain what your dots show for each case. Say why you cannot see the parts.
answer: Case A: the same dots before and after, closer together while the cushion is flat; the sealed cushion still holds the air. Case B: dots of the solid spread through the water; clear water does not mean the solid is gone. Each case earns four points: retained matter, explanatory arrangement, unseen scale and an explanation linked to the evidence. 8 points in all.
steps: Case A, retained matter: the same dots in the cushion before and after, none vanish | Case A, arrangement: the dots are closer together in less space while flat | Case A, unseen scale: dots stand for parts too small to see, not visible grains | Case A, evidence: the explanation uses the sealed, flattened cushion to say the air is still there | Case B, retained matter: dots of the solid are drawn after it spreads, not gone | Case B, arrangement: the dots of the solid are spread through the water | Case B, unseen scale: dots are smaller than any grain; clear water does not mean nothing is there | Case B, evidence: the explanation uses the sealed pouch and the clear water to say the solid is still inside
samples: Dots stand for parts smaller than grains. The cushion keeps all its parts in less space. The solid's parts spread through the water. Becoming clear does not prove disappearance. | Nothing remains inside either.

stem: Your group has a sealed pouch of water that was chilled. Its first reading is on the card beside it. Zero the empty scale. Weigh the whole pouch now that it has warmed. Read it twice. Write the reading in whole grams. Compare it with the card. Write what the two readings say about the matter in the pouch.
answer: The empty scale is zeroed, the whole pouch is weighed, a whole-gram value holds on the second reading, and the comparison says the matter was kept, within the limit of a scale that reads whole grams. 4 points, one for each. Score the child's actual readings and reasoning, not exact agreement.
steps: zeroes the empty scale before weighing | weighs the whole pouch, not only the water | records a stable whole-gram value that holds on a second reading | says what the comparison shows about retained matter, with the limit of the scale
samples: I zeroed the scale. The whole dry pouch settled at 104 g on two readings, matching the earlier 104 g. No change was detected within the scale's whole-gram limit, so the readings support retained matter through warming. | I weighed only the water.

stem: After pumping, will the flat ball weigh more, less or the same? Write why.
answer: A prediction (more, less or the same) with a reason. Any prediction is fine here; the readings will test it.
steps: a prediction is written: more, less or the same | a reason is given
samples: More. Air will go in, and I think air is something. | The same. Air is nothing, so it cannot add weight.

stem: The teacher weighs the flat ball, pumps it, and weighs it again. Write both readings in grams. Then write how many grams the ball gained.
answer: Record actual whole-gram readings twice. If stable, subtract the flat reading from the pumped reading. An unresolved or unstable change is flagged, never forced. Invented N1 gives 424 - 420 = 4 g.
steps: record actual flat and pumped readings in grams | check repeated readings and flag unresolved changes | for a stable comparison subtract flat from pumped; invented N1 gives 4 g
samples: Flat 420 g. Pumped 424 g. The ball gained 4 g. | Flat 420 g. Pumped 424 g. The ball is the same weight.

stem: Draw what went into the ball. Show what made it heavier.
answer: A drawing with something going into or sitting inside the ball, linked to the gain in grams.
steps: something is drawn going into or inside the ball, not an empty ball | the drawing or a label links it to the gain in grams
samples: Arrows go into the ball, labeled air. The ball got heavier because air went in. | A ball with nothing drawn inside. Air is nothing.

stem: Add dots to your drawing. Each dot is a part too small to see. Write what your dots show.
answer: Dots drawn in the ball, and a sentence that says the dots are parts too small to see.
steps: dots are drawn in the ball | the sentence says the dots are parts of air too small to see, not grains you could pick up
samples: Dots are all through the ball. Each dot is a part of air too small to see. | Each dot is one grain of sand that you can see.

stem: Rebuild your six pieces into a new object. Write how many pieces before and after. Finish: This piece helps because ___ so the ___ can ___.
answer: Six before and six after. The sentence links one piece's shape to the job it does, with because or so.
steps: six pieces before and six after, none left out | the sentence links a piece's shape to its job with because or so
samples: 6 before and 6 after. This block helps because it is long and flat, so the ramp can hold a toy car. | 6 before and 5 after. Long is good.

stem: Blocks show parts and wholes. Say one thing blocks cannot show about the parts of air.
answer: Blocks are big and we can see them. They cannot show how small the parts of air are.
steps: says the real parts are far too small to see or far smaller than a block
samples: The parts of air are much smaller than a block, too small to see. | Blocks show air exactly.

stem: Six numbered blocks make a tower. Rebuild them as a low wall. Point to block 3 and explain its job.
answer: All six remain. Block 3 may support the wall or fill a gap; explain its actual position.
steps: locate all six blocks | point to block 3 | link its shape or position to its job
samples: Block 3 fills a gap. Its flat base rests on the block below. | Block 3 was left out.

stem: Build something with six blocks. Rebuild it as another thing. For each block number, write the job it does now.
answer: All six block numbers appear, each with a job in the new object.
steps: all six blocks are listed, none left out and none added | each block has a job in the new object
samples: 1 and 2 are the legs. 3 is the top. 4, 5 and 6 hold the sides. | 1, 2, 3 and 4 are the table.

stem: Invented for practice. A tray holds damp soil. Someone labels the whole reading dry soil. Explain what that reading includes.
answer: It includes the tray, soil and water. Tare the tray and establish an air-dried baseline before adding water.
steps: identify tray, soil and water | exclude tray by taring | establish an air-dried soil baseline
samples: The reading includes the tray and damp soil. Zero the tray and dry the soil first. | The whole reading is dry soil.

stem: Invented for practice. A closed syringe reads 20 mL, then 12 mL. Explain this using one dotted model and labels.
answer: One annotated model shows unseen air parts. The smaller space needs closer spacing while air remains enclosed.
steps: draw one dotted air model | label dots as unseen parts | explain smaller space with closer spacing, not fewer parts
samples: Dots show unseen parts. They sit closer when the marked space decreases. No air was released. | Less space means air vanished.

stem: Read your syringe before and after a gentle press. Write both volumes in mL. Explain what the readings show.
answer: Two readings at the syringe marks. Air occupies less space under pressure while the tip stays closed.
steps: record readings with mL | link smaller volume to less occupied space | cite closed tip
samples: The marked volume fell while the tip stayed closed. Air took less space. | The air disappeared.

stem: Write one thing you saw that shows the syringe was not empty.
answer: A reading or something seen, such as the plunger stopping at a volume or pushing back, that shows something was inside.
steps: cites a reading or something seen | links it to something being inside the syringe
samples: The plunger stopped at 11 mL and pushed back, so air was inside. | It was empty.

stem: Measure from the stick base to its shadow tip. Write the length in cm. Record the place, date and clock time.
answer: A whole-centimeter length, or unreadable if no clear tip, with fixed place, date and clock time.
steps: align ruler zero with stick base | read nearest centimeter | record place, date and clock time; flag unreadable tips
samples: Invented example: 62 cm; spot A; November 24; 1 pm. | Shadow: long.

stem: Put your day 1 and day 3 drawings side by side. Write one thing that stayed the same and one that changed.
answer: Air remains present in both accounts. The ball gained air; the closed syringe changed occupied space. Dot counts need not match across different apparatus.
steps: identify air in both accounts | distinguish added air from compression of enclosed air
samples: Both contain air. Pumping adds air; pressing a closed syringe changes its space. | Every container must have the same dot count.

stem: Invented for practice. An empty pot is zeroed. Dry soil gives 172 g. Two beans give 174 g. Water gives 204 g. Explain how each added amount can be recovered.
answer: Dry soil 172 g, beans 2 g, water 30 g. Subtract the preceding reading from each new reading.
steps: soil = 172 g after taring | beans = 174 - 172 = 2 g | water = 204 - 174 = 30 g
samples: The beans add 2 g and water adds 30 g. | Beans add 174 g and water adds 204 g.

stem: Revisit the syringe evidence. Revise one air model with labels. Finish: I changed ___ because ___ showed ___.
answer: One annotated model links smaller syringe volume to closer unseen air parts. It retains air and cites the observed or invented record.
steps: retain air in the closed syringe | explain closer spacing using the volume record | label dots as parts too small to see
samples: I changed the spacing because the closed syringe reading fell. Dots show unseen air parts. | I removed dots because the air disappeared.

stem: Use the pot log. Zero the empty pot. Record each reading and the grams added for soil, beans and water.
answer: Actual whole-gram readings and differences. Do not predict seed mass. Record unresolved additions as below resolution, not exact zero.
steps: tare empty pot | record air-dried baseline | subtract successive readings | flag unstable or unresolved readings
samples: Invented: soil 164 g; after beans 167 g, 3 g added; after water 195 g, 28 g added. | Soil 164 g; beans 167 g; water 195 g.

stem: Invented for practice. Source P: Added powder becomes invisible in water. Filtering leaves no visible powder. Source R: Drying that filtered liquid leaves solid. Drying plain water leaves none. Revise a liquid model using evidence from both records.
answer: Distributed unseen parts pass the filter and remain in the liquid. P supports passage; R supports retention with plain water as comparison. Dots are smaller than grains.
steps: retains distributed unseen material below grain scale | cites both P and R, including the plain-water comparison
samples: My inset keeps unseen parts throughout the water. P reports clear filtrate; R recovers solid only from the mixture. | The clear liquid contains no powder.

stem: Invented for practice. A sealed jar holds a clear solution. Cooling produces crystals. Warming makes them disappear from view again. Make an evidence-labeled model testing whether the dissolved solid stopped existing.
answer: Model retained dissolved parts in the clear stage. Crystal recovery and repeated disappearance from view inside the sealed jar support persistence. No microscopic temperature mechanism required.
steps: models retained unseen parts in clear liquid | uses both crystal recovery on cooling and disappearance from view on warming
samples: My inset keeps unseen solid parts. Crystals return, then become invisible again in the sealed jar. | The solid is destroyed each time it becomes clear.

stem: Invented for practice. A tire is squeezed with its valve closed. Clear mineral water leaves solid after drying. Make one evidence-labeled model explaining both cases at an unseen scale.
answer: Tire retains air in less space; dissolved mineral remains distributed in clear water and is recovered on drying. Dots stand for parts far smaller than grains.
steps: retains air in less space and mineral distributed in water | cites closed valve and recovered solid | distinguishes unseen parts from visible grains
samples: The closed tire keeps unseen air in less space. Mineral parts remain in water, as dried solid shows. Dots are smaller than grains. | The tire is empty and the mineral vanished.

stem: Invented for practice. A holder tips a soluble tablet into water. Plan a comparison using one whole-gram scale. Draw everything you would weigh twice, and explain your boundary.
answer: Same scale, cup, water, tablet and holder before and after. Include the initially separate tablet and retain all apparatus.
steps: draws complete before/after boundaries with initially separate tablet and holder | justifies retained apparatus and same whole-gram scale
samples: Both tray outlines include cup, water, tablet and holder. Retaining everything makes the comparison fair. | I discard the holder afterward.

stem: Invented for practice. Solid pellets melt inside a sealed pack on a tray. Complete tray and pack: 92 g before; 92 g after. Melted contents alone: 80 g. Make a labeled evidence graph testing whether melting lost matter.
answer: Equal complete-system bars at 92 g from zero in grams. Annotate tray and pack included twice; no detected total change at this scale step.
steps: selects complete totals and plots equal labeled 92 g bars on zero-based gram axes | links unchanged boundary to no detected total loss
samples: Both bars reach 92 g. Tray and pack were included twice, so no total change was detected. | My after bar is 80 g because only contents count.

stem: Invented for practice. A pouch and sleeve weigh 110 g before freezing. Afterward, the frozen pouch weighs 100 g. Its unchanged sleeve weighs 10 g. Graph comparable totals and judge whether cooling removed matter.
answer: 100 + 10 = 110 g afterward. Two complete 110 g bars from zero in grams; no detected loss.
steps: reconstructs and graphs complete 110 g totals | connects unchanged boundary and readings to no detected cooling loss
samples: 100 + 10 = 110 g. Both complete bars reach 110 g, showing no detected loss. | Freezing removed 10 g, so I graph 100 g.

stem: Invented for practice. A clear sugar mixture has two records. Sealed apparatus: 98 g before stirring; 98 g after. Poured-out liquid alone: 86 g. Make an evidence graph testing matter loss and locating the sugar.
answer: Use equal 98 g complete-apparatus bars from zero in grams. Sugar remains unseen throughout liquid. The 86 g boundary differs.
steps: selects and graphs complete 98 g totals | locates retained unseen sugar and explains unchanged total
samples: Both complete bars reach 98 g. Sugar remains unseen in liquid; the liquid-only record omits apparatus. | Sugar vanished, so I use 86 g afterward.

stem: Invented for practice. Both plans repeat three open trials and three balloon trials. Amounts and scale stay the same. Plan A removes the powder holder afterward. Plan B retains every part and checks spills. Judge the fair plan and explain why lower open readings still need checking.
answer: B retains complete apparatus. Lower readings could also reflect spills, apparatus changes or scale problems. Name an alternative and relevant controlled check.
steps: chooses B because every part remains | names an alternative cause and a controlled check
samples: B retains the holder. A spill could lower the reading; inspect the tray and reweigh complete dry apparatus. | Removing the holder is fair; every decrease proves gas escape.

stem: Invented for practice. An open fizzing system reads 135 g, then 134 g. A gas-retaining system reads 137 g twice. Records rule out spills and apparatus changes. Graph both records and model possible matter routes.
answer: Plot 135/134 g open and 137/137 g retaining on zero-based gram axes. Model gas crossing open boundary, retained inside collector boundary. Supports escape without uniquely proving it; no fixed count of particle types through reaction required.
steps: plots both pairs accurately with gram labels | models gas as matter crossing open boundary and retained inside collector
samples: My open bars reach 135 and 134 g; retaining bars reach 137 g. Unseen gas can leave the open boundary but stays within the collector. | Gas has no matter.

stem: Invented for practice. Record A: A collector gains 2 g as its gas-releasing bottle loses 2 g. Record B: A spill tray gains 3 g as its cup loses 3 g. Record C: An empty scale reads 2 g. Record D: An unchanged pouch reads 4 g more on an added tray. Match each record to its supported cause. Choose one row and propose a fair remeasurement.
answer: A gas transfer across bottle boundary; B spilled liquid across cup boundary; C zero error; D changed apparatus. Use unchanged complete boundary or zero/check scale and reweigh, matching chosen row.
steps: matches all four records to supported causes | proposes one relevant controlled remeasurement
samples: A gas transfer; B spill; C scale zero; D added apparatus. For D, reweigh the same pouch and tray both times. | All four prove gas escape; the tray never counts.

stem: Invented for practice. A sealed food pack warms: 72 g before and after. Sealed juice cools: 81 g before and after. Sweetener mixes inside a sealed pack: 94 g before and after. Revise the blank model to explain all three patterns and unseen matter.
answer: All complete sealed boundaries retain matter. Unseen parts are smaller than grains, including dissolved sweetener. Equal pairs support no detected change, not exact equality below instrument step.
steps: models retained matter across all three records | distinguishes unseen parts from grains, including dissolved sweetener | links equal pairs to no detected total change
samples: Each boundary keeps unseen parts through change. Sweetener parts remain spread throughout liquid. Equal pairs support no detected total change. | Warming creates matter and clear sweetener stops existing.

stem: Invented for practice. Heating: complete wax pouch and sleeve, 134 g before. Melted pouch alone, 122 g after; unchanged sleeve, 12 g. Cooling: sealed wax tin, 138 g before and after. A draft graph drops from 138 g to 124 g because wax shrank. Mixing: sealed pouch and contents, 145 g before. Contents alone, 130 g after; empty pouch, 15 g. Make evidence-labeled before-and-after graphs for all three changes using complete totals. Correct the cooling draft within your graph.
answer: Heating 122 + 12 = 134 g, so 134/134 g. Cooling 138/138 g; shrinking changes space, not recorded total. Mixing 130 + 15 = 145 g, so 145/145 g. Six points: one matching complete graph and one evidence-linked explanation per change.
steps: heating graph 134/134 g | heating explanation includes sleeve, 122 + 12 = 134 g | cooling graph corrects draft to 138/138 g | cooling explanation separates space from amount | mixing graph 145/145 g | mixing explanation includes pouch, 130 + 15 = 145 g
samples: Graphs: 134/134, 138/138, 145/145 g. Adding sleeve and pouch restores complete totals. Shrinking does not change the recorded total. | Warming creates matter; packaging does not count.

stem: Invented for practice. A complete sealed pouch reads 156 g, then 153 g. An unchanged check weight reads 50 g before and 47 g afterward. Explain the pattern and propose a fair remeasurement.
answer: Both fall 3 g: 156 - 153 = 3 and 50 - 47 = 3. A possible common scale offset, not proof of lost pouch matter. Zero and verify scale with unchanged check object, then reweigh complete dry pouch. Two points.
steps: identifies paired 3 g drops as evidence of possible scale offset | proposes zero/check then reweighing complete pouch
samples: Both fell 3 g, suggesting a scale problem. Zero and verify the scale, then reweigh the complete pouch. | The lower reading certainly proves gas escaped.

stem: Invented for practice. A sealed empty-looking float keeps water outside. Draw what occupies it and explain its unseen scale.
answer: Unseen air occupies the float. Dots represent parts smaller than visible grains.
steps: shows air occupying float | explains unseen scale
samples: Air fills it; dots are smaller than grains. | Nothing is inside.

stem: Invented for practice. A sealed sand mixer and cradle read 126 g. After turning, the mixer reads 118 g; its cradle reads 8 g. Graph comparable totals and explain.
answer: 118 + 8 = 126 g. Equal complete 126 g bars from zero in grams; retain cradle both times.
steps: graphs complete 126 g totals | explains unchanged boundary
samples: 118 + 8 = 126 g. Complete totals match with the cradle included. | After total is 118 g.

stem: Invented for practice. A sealed gel pack changes appearance while cooling. Complete readings are 113 g twice. Graph the evidence with a conservation caption.
answer: Equal 113 g complete bars from zero in grams; no detected total loss through cooling.
steps: graphs equal labeled 113 g bars | links complete readings to retention
samples: Both complete bars reach 113 g. No total loss was detected. | Cooling removes matter.

stem: Invented for practice. A supplied record shows clear cleaner liquid drying to solid. Draw its earlier clear stage with an evidence caption.
answer: Retained dissolved parts throughout clear liquid, supported by recovered solid. Paper only; no cleaner handled.
steps: models retained unseen dissolved material | cites recovered solid
samples: Clear liquid still held unseen parts, as the recovered solid shows. | The cleaner stopped existing.

stem: Invented for practice. A closed liquid kit reads 108 g, then 105 g. No spill, leak or scale checks were recorded. Explain why the drop alone cannot identify escaping gas.

steps: identifies missing control | explains why an alternative remains possible
samples: Nobody checked scale zero; a scale problem remains possible. | Every fall proves gas escape.

stem: Invented for practice. Matched bean plants receive different water amounts. Other shown conditions stay the same. The watered plant grows more. Explain how these surroundings could affect the shown growth.

stem: Invented for practice. Pond plants vanish. An invented grazer depends on those plants for food. Explain how this change could affect its survival.

answer: Locates original ball readings supporting added air, syringe readings supporting retained air in less space, and dried-dish comparison supporting retained salt. Labels distinguish visible grains from unseen parts; no combined written practice model.

samples: Three groups per condition use equal portions and retain everything. Spills stop the trial. | Remove any unused supports.
